Merevale
MEER-vayl
n. (a Cistercian abbey in Warwickshire, founded 1148 as a daughter of Bordesley; its gate chapel survives as the parish church)
Old English mere, a pool or lake, with vale, a valley: the valley of the pool.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Merevale was founded in 1148 in north Warwickshire, a daughter of Bordesley, and little of the abbey proper survives beyond fragments and earthworks. Its gate chapel does survive, entire, and has been the parish church of Merevale since the dissolution — the same arrangement as at Kirkstead, with the opposite outcome, since here the lay chapel was not merely left standing but taken over as the congregation's own. Having stated the objection to gate chapels under Kirkstead, this entry states the better half of the story: the building put up to keep the laity at the gate became the building in which the laity are the church. That is the Reformation in one parish, and Scripture supplies the warrant for the whole direction of travel: “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1Pe 2:9). A people called a priesthood needs no outer court.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines chapel as a place of worship subordinate to a parish church; parish as the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church; and priesthood as the office or character of a priest, and the order of men set apart for sacred offices.

expand to see more

CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; a place of worship subordinate to a parish church, or annexed to a mansion or castle.

PARISH, n. The precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church; also, the inhabitants themselves.

PRIESTHOOD, n. The office or character of a priest; also, the order of men set apart for sacred offices.

MERE, n. A pool or lake; a standing water; also, a boundary.

VALE, n. A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.

Key Scripture

1Pe 2:9 — "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:"

1Pe 2:5 — "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ."

Rev 1:6 — "And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen."

Eph 2:19 — "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;"

Modern Corruption

A Warwickshire house of 1148 whose gate chapel for the laity became, and remains, the parish church: a building raised to keep people out, now the church they are.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the priesthood of all believers, which is not a slogan but a text: “And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen” (Rev 1:6). Everything the gate chapel implied about degrees of access is answered by it.

The live corruption is the quiet return of a clerical caste in Protestant dress: the professional who prays, studies and administers while the congregation watches. “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices” (1Pe 2:5) gives the whole body the offering to make, and “Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (Eph 2:19) settles the standing of everyone in the room.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hierateuma (G2406), a priesthood; Greek laos (G2992), a people; Greek sumpolites (G4847), a fellowcitizen; Greek oikeios (G3609), of the household; Hebrew mamlakah (H4467), a kingdom.

expand to see more

Greek hierateuma (G2406) — a priesthood; “a royal priesthood, an holy nation” (1Pe 2:9).

Greek laos (G2992) — a people; the root of laity, and a word of honour.

Greek sumpolites (G4847) — a fellowcitizen; “but fellowcitizens with the saints” (Eph 2:19).

Greek oikeios (G3609) — belonging to a household; the status of every believer.

Greek basileia (G932) — a kingdom; “And hath made us kings and priests unto God” (Rev 1:6).

Usage

"“that ye should shew forth the praises of him” (1Pe 2:9) — the whole people given the work of praise."

"“hath made us kings and priests unto God” (Rev 1:6) — the end of an outer court."

"“ye are no more strangers and foreigners” (Eph 2:19) — the standing of the people at the gate."
